classification.difficultyReason: Two inverse-normal design problems (70% and 99%). The student must choose the percentile and round up to a whole centimetre, which is a small interpretation step. Comparable to the doorway problem.

content.prompt: Adult heights in Australia are approximately normally distributed.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Women's heights have mean 162 cm and standard deviation 6.5 cm. A tram doorway is designed so 70% of women can enter without ducking. Find the minimum doorway height, in whole centimetres.

answer.worked:
We want $P(Z<z)=0.70$. From the table, $P(Z\le0.5)=0.6915$ and $P(Z\le0.6)=0.7257$. Since $0.70$ is about a quarter of the way from $0.6915$ to $0.7257$, $z\approx0.525$.
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\mu+z\sigma\\x&\approx162+0.525(6.5)\\x&\approx165.4\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$Round up to give a minimum whole-centimetre height of $166\text{ cm}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Men's heights have mean 178 cm and standard deviation 8 cm. A bed is made long enough that only 1% of men are taller than it. Find the minimum bed length, in whole centimetres.

answer.worked:
$P(X\le x)=1-0.01=0.99$, so we want $P(Z<z)=0.99$. From the table, $P(Z\le2.3)=0.9893$ and $P(Z\le2.4)=0.9918$. Since $0.99$ is about $0.28$ of the way from $0.9893$ to $0.9918$, $z\approx2.33$.
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\mu+z\sigma\\x&\approx178+2.33(8)\\x&\approx196.6\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$Round up to give a minimum whole-centimetre length of $197\text{ cm}$.
